prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The first-round exchange has sharpened the case instead of weakening it. The physical idea is simple to picture: at the magic wavelength the trapping light shifts the two clock levels by the same amount, so the trap does not disturb the frequency, and the atoms are held tightly enough that Doppler and recoil effects disappear. That lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, which is what gives both the signal-to-noise and the accuracy. The result is verified in the way I trust most. Independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) compare their clocks over fibre links at the 1e-18 level, and the agreement is not a claim from one apparatus. It also says something about nature: gravitational redshift is resolved across millimetres and the constancy of constants is tested more tightly. I want the citation to be about the lattice clock itself, so that it is neither a repeat of the 2005 comb prize nor a pre-emption of a later nuclear-clock discussion. I stress that seven of eight configurations coincide partly because we read each other's openings, as Kroll and I both said, so I rest my vote on the physics and the attribution, not on the count.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that a clock prize may be read as refinement of precision spectroscopy already honoured in 1989, 2005 and 2012. I do not think it is a bar, but it means the citation must name what is new: magic-wavelength trapping and many-atom interrogation. The second objection, pressed by Olsson, is that the statutes reward the original discovery and not the better later realisation, so Ye's separate credit must be demonstrable. I find the record supports it but not without effort (see my reply to Olsson), and I flag that I am recalling dates and author lists from memory. A third objection is that the fundamental-physics reach (variation of constants, dark matter) is still prospective, as Eriksson and Mehlig note; the lattice clock is a mature measurement result, but the discoveries it enables have not yet been made. Finally, Lemonde and SYRTE, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom, and the Yb, Hg and Al+ communities all have credible claims to part of the story, which three names cannot fully capture.

responses.point: Olsson, backed by the Chair's question, asks what establishes that Ye's contribution is original and decisive in its own right and not an improvement of Katori's invention, and wants the record to separate Ye's results from those of Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and others.
responses.response: I think the answer exists but should be stated precisely. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice (about 2001 to 2003) and his group demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock (Takamoto, Hong, Higashi, Katori, Nature 2005). Ye's contribution is different in kind and, I believe, independently decisive. His group built the Sr lattice clock at JILA (Boyd, Ludlow and others, 2006 to 2008), showed that the lattice clock could reach and pass the accuracy of the best ion and microwave standards, and then took it to 1e-18 (Nicholson 2015, Bloom 2014) through control of blackbody radiation and collisional shifts, with coherence times that make many-body interrogation possible (Campbell 2017, Fermi-degenerate operation and spin-orbit coupled clocks). Hinkley, Ludlow, Bloom and Nicholson were Ye's students and postdocs working on that programme, and in experimental prizes the group leader is credited in that way. I also note that the ultimate performance is exactly what turned a promising idea into the instrument everyone else now copies; without it nobody would be comparing at 1e-18. I mark these dates as recalled from memory. Olsson's rule about the original experiment is met by Katori; for Ye the case is that he made the idea work at the limit and showed which systematics matter, and I would be content if the citation says 'invention and realisation' to reflect the two roles. If colleagues are not persuaded about Ye, the alternative is a Katori-only prize, but I would regard that as less faithful to how the field developed.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B024 (magic-angle graphene) on the grounds that a simple mechanism, the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald flat band, was confirmed by the 2018 experiments, opened a new field of tunable correlated matter, and the pairing question does not undermine the existence of the correlated phases.
responses.response: I find his argument clear and the prediction-then-observation sequence is attractive; I also take it as a sign of respect that he lists B052 first among his alternatives. As an atomic theorist I defer to him on condensed matter, but two things keep me from moving B024 above the clock. First, the credit: Cao is first author of the 2018 papers, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto had earlier twisted-bilayer theory, and Bistritzer and MacDonald share a single paper, so two of three places go to one result. Second, maturity: eight years of experiments with large sample-to-sample variation and an unexplained superconducting mechanism is shorter than the replication record of the clocks. I do not say the field is unimportant, and I would not be surprised to see a prize there within some years. If his preference rests on discovery type, I would say a new correlated state is indeed discovery in the strict sense, and I am open to this being the better prize in a year when the credit is resolved. For this year I stay with B052 because I can defend every name.

responses.point: Kroll agrees on B052 and on the caution about B035, adds that Chu's light-pulse work sits at the centre of the Kasevich story so the Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich trio is defensible but not clean, and that a B052 plus single B035 name would be arbitrary.
responses.response: I agree and the point on the arbitrary single name closes the question for me on any two-part configuration this year. I would add that a two-part prize must not be driven by the fact that atom interferometry and the lattice clock are both precision quantum measurement and are close to our own field. That is a reason for caution, not for a combined prize. I therefore decline a second part, and I keep B035 only as an alternative. Our near-identical openings should not be counted twice, which is why I try here to give reasons that do not depend on his.

responses.point: Danielsson states that difficulty of attribution is the committee's problem and not a verdict on the science, and does not want a statute limit of three people to decide what counts as important; he still lists the Higgs observation as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree with that principle, and I did not rank B010 lower because the physics is less important; it is the most important result on our list. My point is narrower: the prize cannot be given to an experiment that we cannot credit faithfully. If the committee later finds a formulation that reflects the 2012 observation fairly, I would take it seriously as a candidate. I do not think it is helpful for this round to hold a first-class discovery against a first-class clean one in a ranking whose result is decided by the statute. I would also say, to his earlier worry about instrumentation, that the magic wavelength is a result about atomic structure and not just a tool, and that is why I regard the lattice clock as a discovery in the sense the will intends.

responses.point: Eriksson says the distinction from the 2005 comb prize is real and asks that Ye's description be careful so that it does not read like a comb prize, and notes that the fundamental-physics reach is still largely prospective.
responses.response: I accept both points and have changed the citation wording accordingly: it now says 'based on magic-wavelength trapping' so that the object recognised is the lattice clock. On the prospective reach, I agree that no variation of constants or dark-matter signal has been seen, and I would not allow the citation to promise one. What exists is a measurement of redshift over millimetres and new bounds, which is already a result. I also repeat that the 1e-18 agreement among independent clocks is the reason I find the maturity convincing; it does not depend on a future discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's separate and decisive contribution can be shown to the committee's satisfaction without relying on my recollection of the JILA publication record; I have not verified the dates and author lists.
Whether other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde and SYRTE, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom, and the Yb, Hg and Al+ groups) deserve credit that a two-name citation overrides.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize, and whether later nuclear-clock work by Ye should affect timing.
Whether B035 can ever be given a defensible three-name set without Chu, and whether B044 can be given a fair split between the theory proposal (Zoller, Jaksch) and the experiments.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I have no recorded collaboration with Katori or Ye, and my collaborators (L'Huillier, the Keller group, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) are not among the credited names on B052. For transparency, I am a long-time collaborator of 2023 laureate Anne L'Huillier and work in atomic theory, which is adjacent to precision atomic metrology. This is not a tie to any credited name on a shortlisted ballot that I put forward, so I do not think recusal is needed, but I would recuse on any configuration that included a direct collaborator.
